One of the most common warm-up questions in system design interviews:

Design a service like bit.ly. Users submit a long URL and get a short one, like lt.io/aZ3k9Q. Anyone opening the short link is redirected to the original. Expect 100 million new links a month and 100 times more clicks than new links.

The Numbers First

  • 100 million links a month is about 40 writes per second.
  • 100 times more reads: about 4,000 redirects per second, more at peak.
  • At 500 bytes per link, a year of links is 100 M × 12 × 500 B = 600 GB: one database can hold that.
  • Base62 codes (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) of 7 characters give 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion possible codes.

So this is a read-heavy system with modest storage. The hard parts are generating unique codes and serving redirects fast.

The Naive Version

Hash the long URL and keep the first 7 characters:

import hashlib

def short_code(long_url):
    digest = hashlib.md5(long_url.encode()).hexdigest()
    return digest[:7]

It breaks in two ways:

  • Collisions. Two different URLs can share the first 7 characters. You must check the database on every create, and pick another code when it's taken.
  • Same URL, same code. Two users shortening the same link get the same code, so one user's expiry date or statistics affect the other.

Generating Unique Codes

Give each link a unique number, then encode the number in base62:

ALPHABET = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"

def base62(number):
    code = ""
    while number > 0:
        number, rest = divmod(number, 62)
        code = ALPHABET[rest] + code
    return code or "0"

A unique number can't collide, so no check is needed. Where do the numbers come from?

  • A database sequence. Simple, but a single counter is a bottleneck and a single point of failure.
  • Ranges. A small coordination service hands each app server a block, like 1 to 1,000,000. The server uses its block from memory, then asks for the next one. Losing a server only wastes the rest of its block.
  • Snowflake-style IDs. Each server builds 64-bit IDs from a timestamp, its worker number and a counter, with no coordination at all.

Sequential codes are easy to guess: someone can walk through aZ3k9Q, aZ3k9R… and find private links. If that matters, shuffle the bits of the number with a reversible function before encoding, or add a few random characters.

The Design

Client → Load balancer → Link service → Cache (Redis) → Database
                              ↓
                       ID ranges service

Creating a link: the link service takes the next number from its range, encodes it, stores code → long_url in the database and returns the short URL.

Following a link: the service looks the code up in the cache, then in the database on a miss, and answers with a redirect. A few popular links get most of the clicks, so a cache of the hottest links absorbs most of the reads.

The servers keep no state, so you add servers behind the load balancer as traffic grows.

301 or 302?

Redirect Browser behavior Good for
301 Cached: later clicks may skip your server Less load, permanent links
302 Every click comes back to your server Click counts, editable links

Most shorteners use 302 (or 307), because statistics and the ability to change or disable a link matter more than the saved requests.

Counting Clicks Without Slowing Redirects

Updating a counter row on every click puts a write in the hot path, and popular links turn one row into a bottleneck. Instead, the redirect sends a small click event to a queue and returns immediately. Workers read the queue and update counts in batches, every few seconds.

Every Failure, and What Happens

What goes wrong What happens Result
Cache is down Every redirect reads the database Slower, but works if the database can take the load
A link server crashes The load balancer stops sending it traffic Its unused ID range is skipped; no duplicates
ID ranges service is down Servers keep using the ranges they hold New ranges wait; existing ones last a while
Click queue is slow Events wait in the queue Counts lag; redirects stay fast
A link is deleted The cache may still hold it Delete the cache key too, or wait for its TTL

Details Interviewers Ask About

  • Custom aliases. lt.io/summer-sale must be checked for uniqueness on create, and kept apart from generated codes, for example with a reserved prefix or a minimum length.
  • Expiry. Store expires_at, check it on every redirect, and delete expired links in the background.
  • Abuse. Check new URLs against lists of malware and phishing sites, and rate limit creation per user or IP.
  • Several regions. Replicate links to read replicas near users; writes can go to one primary, since they're rare.
  • Sharding. Not needed at 600 GB a year. If it grows, shard by code: every redirect knows its code, so it knows its shard.

The Answer in Short

  1. Estimate first: about 40 writes and 4,000 reads per second, 600 GB a year.
  2. Give each link a unique number from pre-allocated ranges, and encode it in base62.
  3. Store code → long_url in a database, with the code as the key.
  4. Serve redirects through a cache, from stateless servers behind a load balancer.
  5. Use 302 to keep click statistics, and count clicks through a queue, in batches.
  6. Add custom aliases, expiry and abuse checks as extras.
